claims.text: Room-temperature plastic deformation in the quaternary equiatomic FCC alloy will be dominated by dislocation glide on {111} planes.
Deformation twinning may accompany glide depending on stacking-fault energy.
An FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation may accompany glide depending on stacking-fault energy.
Yield strength will be governed by the initial dislocation density.
Yield strength will be governed by solid-solution strengthening.
Yield strength may become insensitive to strain rate at approximately 300–500 K.
A transition to thermally activated dislocation climb can cause strain-rate insensitivity.
Twinning or martensite formation is less rate-sensitive than pure dislocation glide.
Strain-rate insensitivity is reached when thermal energy is sufficient to overcome a Peierls barrier for dislocation climb.
Strain-rate insensitivity can arise when phase-transformation kinetics become rate-limiting.
Lomer-Cottrell locks observed in nanowire studies may impede dislocation glide in the target alloy.
Dislocation glide and twinning are the primary room-temperature mechanisms in FCC equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
Twinning and martensitic transformation can activate simultaneously during tension at 300 K.
Stress-assisted dislocation climb and dynamic recrystallization dominate at higher temperatures and reduce strain-rate sensitivity.
Twinning and/or TRIP at higher strains enhance work hardening.
Yield strength will decrease as temperature increases.
At room temperature, significant work hardening will result from dislocation accumulation and possible twinning.
At 400–600 K, a stress-strain plateau or reduced slope will indicate strain-rate insensitivity caused by climb or phase transformation.
Pure dislocation glide produces a power-law strain-rate exponent of approximately 0.02–0.05.
For CoCrFeNi, the strain-rate-insensitivity boundary is likely above 400–500 K.

contradictions.description: The proposed climb-controlled boundary is placed at 300–600 K, whereas the cited creep evidence concerns 500–600 °C (773–873 K). The Celsius-to-kelvin temperature mismatch is not acknowledged, so the cited high-temperature mechanism does not ground the stated boundary.
